sections.title: 1. Socrates
blocks: Core Definition: "Philosophy" means the love of wisdom. Understanding the self allows us to know who we are and become better.
Method of Study: The self is best understood through introspection and questioning .
The Soul: Considered the true self, distinct from the body, immortal, and the source of moral and intellectual virtues. Focuses on the full power of reason in the human self.
Core Questions: ○ Who are we? ○ Whom should we be? ○ Whom will we become?
Key Principles: ○ Virtue comes from knowledge. ○ Socratic Method: Questioning as a path to self-knowledge.
Famous Maxim: "An unexamined life is not worth living."

sections.title: 2. Plato
blocks: Famous Maxim: "Know Thyself" .
Dualism of Man: A human being is made up of: ○ Body: Physical, temporary, belonging to the material world. ○ Soul: Eternal, rational, true self, belonging to the Realm of Forms.
Realm of Forms: A hidden, eternal world of perfect ideas, including concepts like beauty, justice, and goodness. When the soul entered the body, it forgot much of this knowledge.
Theory of Recollection: Learning is simply remembering what the soul already knew.

Three Parts of the Soul: ○ Reason: Thinks logically and seeks the truth. Example: Studying instead of procrastinating because you know it's beneficial. ○ Spirit: Produces courage, ambition, and determination. Example: Standing up for a classmate who is being bullied. ○ Appetite: Desires pleasure and physical satisfaction. Example: Wanting junk food, excessive gaming, or unnecessary spending.

The Healthy Self & Well-being (Diagram Breakdown): ○ Reason finds/guides. ○ Spirit supports reason. ○ Appetite is kept under control. ○ Harmony leads to well-being . If human beings do not live in accordance with their nature or function, the result is injustice.
Education Helps the Soul: People who see only shadows mistake appearances for reality. Education helps them "leave the cave" and understand deeper truths (moving beyond what you see on the surface).

sections.title: 3. Aristotle
blocks: Core Definition: The self is a combination (unity) of body and soul. ○ Body: Physical aspect of the person. ○ Soul: Gives meaning and purpose ( telos ).

Types of Souls Table: ○ Nutritive Soul: Found in Plants | Function: Growth, nutrition, reproduction. ○ Sensitive Soul: Found in Animals | Function: Sensation, movement, desire. ○ Rational Soul: Found in Humans | Function: Reasoning, reflection, moral decision-making.

Human Flourishing ( Eudaimonia ): ○ Humans flourish by fulfilling their highest function. ○ Eudaimonia is the goal of life ( Eu = good, daimon = spirit or god). ○ Reason makes us truly human. Understanding yourself means developing that capacity to reason. ○ Knowing what is right is not enough; virtue must be developed through habit.

The Golden Mean: Virtue is balanced between two extremes. ○ Cowardice ↔ Courage (Virtue) ↔ Recklessness ○ Stinginess ↔ Generosity (Virtue) ↔ Wastefulness ○ Shyness ↔ Confidence (Virtue) ↔ Arrogance ○ Laziness ↔ Diligence (Virtue) ↔ Workaholism ○ Self-indulgence ↔ Temperance (Virtue) ↔ Overindulgence MODULE 2: MEDIEVAL TO MODERN PHILOSOPHERS

sections.title: 4. St. Augustine
blocks: Background: African philosopher, regarded as a saint in the Catholic Church. (Note/Fan ni Plato)

Understanding the Self: ○ Involves looking inward and recognizing our relationship with God. ○ Human beings are created by God and possess a spiritual nature. Everything created by God, who is all good, is good. ○ Inner self (soul) > External appearances (body) ○ We are free, but our choices matter.

Methods & Desires: ○ Self-reflection helps discover desires, weaknesses, and our need for God through prayer and confession . ○ Human beings naturally search for happiness and fulfillment through success, money, relationships, pleasure, and achievements, but these only provide temporary satisfaction.

Famous Maxim: "Our hearts are restless until they rest in you." (Confessions) Application Scenario (Exam Dilemma): Scenario: Tomorrow you have a major exam, but your friends invite you to an overnight outing.
Socrates: Have you honestly examined why you're making this decision?
Plato: Which part of the soul is making the decision—reason, spirit, or appetite?
Aristotle: What would be the balanced, virtuous choice that will help you flourish?
St. Augustine: Does this choice align with your spiritual nature and inner self rather than temporary pleasures?

sections.title: 5. René Descartes
blocks: Background: French philosopher, known as the father of modern philosophy .
Method of Doubt: Questioned everything he could doubt until he found one thing he cannot doubt— thinking as proof of one's existence.

Dualism: ○ Self (Soul): A thinking mind ( res cogitans ); does the thinking, doubting, and believing. ○ Body: Physical ( res extensa ); occupies space. ○ Note: The soul and body are independent and can exist and function without each other.
Famous Maxim: Cogito, ergo sum ("I think, therefore I am") .

Thought Experiment on Reality: ○ The Dream Argument: You are dreaming you are in your classroom seeing classmates and feeling chairs, then you wake up realizing it wasn't real. How do you know you aren't dreaming right now? ○ (Self-Note/Joke) : "Cognitive miser - ayaw mo lang mag isip".

sections.title: 6. John Locke
blocks: Background: English philosopher.
The Mind at Birth: The human mind is a blank slate ( tabula rasa ) . The self is constructed primarily from sense experiences.

Personal Identity & Continuity: ○ Personal identity is directly connected to consciousness . ○ Memory connects our past self to our present self. ○ Keys to understanding the self: Consciousness and memory.

sections.title: 7. David Hume
blocks: Background: Scottish philosopher.
The Illusion of a Permanent Self: Questioned the idea that there is a single, unchanging self.
Bundle Theory: The self is a bundle of perceptions (a collection of changing thoughts, experiences, and feelings we have over time).
Fleeting Perceptions: Random moments and snapshots from our lives. Self-identity is strictly a mental construct .

sections.title: 8. Immanuel Kant
blocks: Unifying Consciousness: The self is a unified consciousness that makes it possible for us to experience all different things as belonging to one "I" (an active subject, not just a sum of your experiences).
Transcendental Unity of Apperception: Our minds bring everything together.
Two Sides of the Self: ○ Empirical Self: The self we show the world. ○ Noumenal Self: The deeper, unknowable self beyond our senses.

sections.title: 9. Sigmund Freud
blocks: Levels of the Mind: ○ Conscious: Thoughts we are currently aware of. ○ Preconscious: Memories and stored knowledge. ○ Unconscious: Deep, hidden feelings and desires. Much of who we are lies here.
Three Structures of Personality: ○ Id: Operates on instinctual desires and urges. ○ Ego: The rational part that balances desires with reality. ○ Superego: The moral conscience.

Freudian Slip: An unconscious feeling leaking out. Example: Calling someone you dislike by the name of your ex, then apologizing ("Sorry, I don't know why I said that"). Ethical Responsibility Question:
If there is no permanent self (Hume), what makes you responsible for your past actions? (e.g., A student cheated 10 years ago and is now a completely different person).

Resolution notes: Still connected through the memory of the past . That past connects us to where we are right now. Change happens because of past occurrences, making us accountable for the continuity. MODULE 3: CONTEMPORARY PHILOSOPHERS

sections.title: 10. Gilbert Ryle
blocks: Critique of Dualism: Argued that the mind is not a separate identity or "ghost in the machine." Believed the self is not some inner ghost controlling the body as a separate invisible substance.
Behaviorism: The self manifests in behavior and actions (a pattern of behavior). To understand the self, observe what a person does.

sections.title: 11. Paul Churchland
blocks: Background: Canadian philosopher.
Eliminative Materialism: The radical claim that our common-sense understanding of the mind called "folk psychology" is a false theory.

The Self is the Brain: Mental states (thoughts, emotions, beliefs) are not separate from the brain. The self consists of brain activities and neural processes, not an immaterial or supernatural entity.

Thought Experiment (Altering the Brain): ○ If future technology alters your brain, your fear disappears, memories change, and personality shifts—did they change your brain, or did they change you ? ○ Note: According to Churchland, since they changed your brain and the brain is the self, you are still the same entity .

sections.title: 12. Maurice Merleau-Ponty
blocks: Phenomenology: Focuses on how we experience the world through our bodies.
Perception: The primary way we experience the self and the world.
An Embodied Being: The self is embedded in the body. Bodily experiences shape our identity and how we understand the world around us.
The Body as an Active Agent: An active part of how we perceive and interact with reality.
Self and the World: Our sense of self is shaped by the world, but also shapes how we engage with it (a continuous feedback loop). Thought Experiment (Different Body):
Scenario: If you wake up tomorrow in a different body, your memories, personality, and thoughts are still yours. Would you still be the same person?
Note: You will be a different person because you use the body as an instrument to experience the world.

sections.title: 1. Introduction: The Sociological Perspective
blocks: Core Question: Did society shape you, or did you shape yourself? Before learning who we are independently, we must look at who we are as part of society.

Social Sciences Overview: Systematic study of human behavior and society: ○ Psychology: Study of human behavior and mental processes (e.g., What thoughts, emotions, and personality influence this student? ). ○ Economics: Study of production, distribution, and consumption (e.g., How can financial circumstances influence them? ). ○ Anthropology: Study of culture and human origins (e.g., How does culture affect beliefs and practices? ). ○ Political Science: Study of government and power (e.g., How can the government/political environment affect their life? ). ○ Sociology: Study of human groups, institutions, and social structures (e.g., How can their family and school shape who they are? ).

sections.title: 2. The Traditional View vs. Social Constructivist View
blocks: The Traditional/Independent View (Stevens, 1996): ○ Separate: "Distinct from others" ( Ako, sila , I have my own thoughts and identity, and others have theirs too). ○ Self-Contained & Independent: "In itself can exist"; everything important about me is inside me, like being contained in a box. ○ Consistent & Unitary: "Enduring, can persist"; the self is relatively stable with recurring personality traits. ○ Private: "Within"; if you want to know a person, you have to open the box and look inside.
Sociological Challenge to Independence: Sociology challenges this picture by asking: How independent are we really? How much do family, social media, and culture influence us?

Social Constructivist View: ○ The self is malleable, dynamic, and continuously shaped through social interaction in unceasing flux, through constant interaction with others and adaptation to social life.

sections.title: 3. Marcel Mauss: Two Faces of the Self
blocks: We can adapt to different social contexts without completely losing our sense of who we are. There are two dimensions : 1. Moi (Personal Identity): Who am I? Refers to a person's basic sense of identity, body, individuality, and biological "given-ness." It is what makes us experience ourselves as the same person across time. 2. Personne (Social Identity & Roles): Who am I in society? Refers to social roles, family, religion, nationality, and institutions. It deals with social expectations, norms, and how we learn to behave in different contexts.

Cultural Expressions of Identity (e.g., Filipino Context): Words like "Opo" , "Po" , "Ate/Kuya" signal age, status, closeness, respect, and roles—demonstrating how language, culture, and relationships shape the self.

sections.title: 4. Institutions That Shape the Self
blocks: Self and Family:
Family is our first social world . Humans learn ways of living and their sense of self by being in a family.
What a family initiates a person to become serves as the basis for their progress.
Family shapes: Values, roles, expectations, behaviors, and sense of identity.
Gender and Self:
Gender is a locus of the self subject to alteration, change, and development.
Society forces a particular identity upon us depending on our sex and/or gender.
Important Note: Learning an expectation does not mean we have to accept it.

sections.title: 5. Sociological Theories of Socialization and the Self
blocks: Gerry Lanuza (Modernity & the Self):
Society shapes us, and we shape our social world (how our actions change the people and environment around us).
Filipino sociologist who wrote The Constitution of the Self .

In modern society, identity is freely chosen rather than dictated by tradition, allowing for greater freedom of self-cultivation and self-realization (though freedom can also lead to alienation and dehumanization).
George Herbert Mead (Development of the Social Self):

The self develops entirely through social interaction across three stages : 1. Preparatory Stage (0–3 years old): Imitation of behavior without understanding. 2. Play Stage (3–5 years old): "I take the role of another" (role-taking). 3. Game Stage (Early school years, 8–9 years old): "I understand multiple roles and expectations."
Generalized Other: The internalized understanding of the expectations of the wider social group or society.
Charles Horton Cooley (The Looking-Glass Self):

Answers how other people become part of how we see ourselves through a three-step process : 1. We imagine how others see us. 2. We imagine how they judge us. 3. We develop feelings about ourselves based on that imagined judgment.

sections.title: 6. Modern vs. Postmodern Societies and Consumption
blocks: Modern Society:
Emphasizes stability and structure .
Developed around industrialization, institutions, science, progress, and order.
Postmodern Society:
Emphasizes flexibility, diversity, and constant change .
Rejects the idea of one stable path, one truth, or one fixed identity.
Jean Baudrillard (The Consumer Self):
French sociologist.
"We don't consume only things. We consume meanings."
People want a product → buy something new → feel good/status.
Products become symbols of status and identity.

sections.title: 1. Self as Embedded in Culture
blocks: Learning Outcomes: ○ Recognize what the field of anthropology can contribute to understanding the self. ○ Understand how culture and self are complementary concepts. ○ Discuss the cultural construction of the self and social identity. ○ Explain the concept of identity struggles. ○ Develop insights on how to achieve a sense of self, situated in multicultural and dynamic situations.

What is Anthropology? ○ Study of humans, their cultures, and how they interact with their environment. ○ Focuses on how societies shape identity and self-perception. ○ Helps us understand that selfhood is culturally constructed and varies across societies.

Clifford Geertz (1973): ○ Culture gives meaning to human experiences. ○ Geertz's key ideas: ■ Culture is not just behaviors or traditions, but a set of rules and instructions for life. ■ Humans rely on culture for guidance and survival. ○ Agreed with Max Weber: Humans create symbols and meanings to organize their world.
Humans as Cultural Animals (Robbins, 2012): ○ Humans create meanings for: Objects, People, Behaviors, Emotions, Events. ○ These meanings shape how we act and interact with others.

sections.title: 2. Cultural Construction of the Self and Identity
blocks: Edward Tylor (1871): ○ Defined culture as a complex whole including knowledge, beliefs, art, morals, laws, and customs. ○ Culture shapes individual identity and behavior.
Martin Sokefeld: ○ Argued that the self is a cultural concept—what it means to be a "self" depends on societal beliefs. ○ Different cultures emphasize either individualism or collectivism.
Social Anthropology and Identity: ○ Identity is shaped by social groups (family, ethnicity, religion, nationality). ○ Ethnic identity: A sense of belonging to a particular ethnic or cultural group.

Peacock (1986): ○ "Individuals are not mere robots nor self an entirely self-willed little god but a cultural individual—existing in freedom but also embodying that cultural mold in which he is cast in his particular society and historical epoch."

sections.title: 3. Egocentric vs. Sociocentric Self
blocks: Egocentric Self (Western view): ○ Self is independent, unique, and responsible for its actions. ○ Egocentric-self is capable of acting independently.
Sociocentric Self (Non-Western view): ○ Self is defined by relationships and social roles. ○ Sociocentric self is context-dependent; no intrinsic self that can possess enduring qualities.

Examples of Sociocentric Self: ○ Christie Kiefer: Japanese culture promotes a sociocentric self—identity depends on social harmony and group belonging. Emphasis on collectivism, duty, and interdependence. ○ Francis Hsu: Chinese self is also sociocentric, shaped by Confucian values. Importance of family, hierarchy, and social responsibility. Self is not isolated but exists within a web of relationships.

sections.title: 4. Identity Toolbox and Personal Naming
blocks: Identity Toolbox: ○ Refers to the features of a person's identity that he or she chooses to emphasize in constructing a social self. ○ Includes gender, ethnicity, language, religion, and social roles. ○ Some aspects are chosen (career, beliefs), while others are assigned (race, family). ○ Other characteristics (personal appearance, socioeconomic status/SES) are not always used in every society.

Personal Naming: ○ Naming is a powerful tool in shaping identity. ○ Establishes birthright, social identity, and belonging. ○ Example (Aymara Indians): Babies are not considered full members of society until they're formally named.

sections.title: 5. Rites of Passage and Identity Struggles
blocks: Three-Phased Rite of Passage (Arnold van Gennep): ○ Changes in one's status and identity are marked by a three-phased rite of passage: 1. Separation: Leaving familiar ground (e.g., moving to a new stage in life). 2. Liminality: The in-between phase (e.g., adolescence training). 3. Incorporation: Fully accepted into the new status (e.g., graduation, marriage).
Wallace and Fogelson (Identity Struggles):
Identity is not fixed—people experience conflicts in self-perception.
Struggles occur when individuals feel torn between cultural expectations.
Katherine Ewing’s Illusion of Wholeness:
In multicultural societies, people adopt multiple self-identities.
Internal conflicts arise when different cultural models contradict each other.
To maintain a stable sense of self, individuals must integrate different cultural influences and suppress or modify certain identities when needed.
Golubovic (2011):
To form a strong sense of self, people must:
Challenge traditions that limit personal growth.
Resist external labels imposed by society.
Develop self-awareness to navigate social expectations.

sections.title: 1. Introduction to Psychology and the Self
blocks: Learning Objectives: ○ Define and describe the different psychological concepts of the self. ○ Differentiate the various concepts of the self and identify their interrelationships. ○ Explain how the concepts of the self influence behavior. ○ Apply concepts of self in one's life to develop self-awareness and self-understanding.

What is Psychology? ○ Studies behavior and mental processes to understand the self. ○ Explores how thoughts, emotions, and behaviors shape identity. ○ Different psychological theories provide perspective on how we develop and define the self.

sections.title: 2. William James - The "I" and the "Me"
blocks: I-self: ○ Subjective self. ○ Thinking, perceiving, experiencing self. ○ Continuously aware and reflective.

Me-self: ○ Objective self. ○ Self that is known and shaped by experiences. ○ Composed of: ■ Material self: physical body, possessions. ■ Social self: how others perceive us. ■ Spiritual self: inner identity, values, beliefs.

sections.title: 3. Carl Rogers - The Self Theory
blocks: Self-Concept: The perception we have of ourselves.
Two Aspects of the Self: ○ Real Self: Who we actually are. ○ Ideal Self: Who we aspire to be.
Congruence vs. Incongruence: ○ Congruence (Ideal Self = Real Self): Normal/healthy self-esteem, well-being. ○ Incongruence (Ideal Self ≠ Real Self): Neurotic/anxiety, self-doubt.
Unconditional Positive Regard: Refers to accepting and supporting someone without judgment or evaluation.

sections.title: 4. Donald Winnicott - Multiple vs. Unified Self, True vs. False Self
blocks: Multiple vs. Unified Self: ○ We present different selves in different contexts. ○ A healthy self integrates these different aspects into a cohesive identity.
True vs. False Self: ○ True Self: Authentic, spontaneous, driven by inner desires. ○ False Self: Created to conform to societal expectations.
When the false self dominates, it can lead to feelings of inauthenticity and distress.

sections.title: 5. Albert Bandura - Self as Proactive and Agentic
blocks: Self as Proactive and Agentic: Self is not passive—we actively shape our own experiences.
Self-efficacy: Belief in one's ability to achieve goals.
Reciprocal determinism: Interaction between behavior, environment, and personal factors.
Observational learning: We learn by watching others (modeling).

sections.title: 6. Carl Jung - Self as Central Archetype
blocks: Self as Central Archetype: The core of personality representing the unified whole of a person.
Individuation / Self-Realization: The ultimate goal of development is self-realization (individuation)—the process of integrating all aspects of the psyche into a balanced self.
Key Archetypes That Shape the Self: ○ Persona: Social mask we wear. ○ Shadow: Hidden, repressed aspects of the self. ○ Anima/Animus: Feminine and masculine aspects within us.

sections.title: 7. Sigmund Freud - Psychoanalytic Perspective
blocks: Three Parts of the Mind: ○ Id: Instinctual drives (pleasure principle). ○ Ego: Rational self (reality principle). ○ Superego: Moral conscience (ideal self).

Personality Development: ○ Shaped by early childhood experiences. ○ Defense mechanisms protect the self from anxiety (e.g., repression, denial, projection). ○ Freud's view: The self is a product of unconscious conflicts between desires, morality, and reality.

sections.title: 8. Erik Erikson - Psychosocial Stages
blocks: Lifespan Development: The self evolves through 8 stages, each with a key challenge.

Stages of Psychosocial Development: 1. Infancy: Trust vs. Mistrust (Foundation of self-security) 2. Early Childhood: Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt 3. Preschool: Initiative vs. Guilt 4. School Age: Industry vs. Inferiority 5. Adolescence: Identity vs. Role Confusion (Success: clear sense of identity; Failure: confusion about self and future roles) 6. Young Adulthood: Intimacy vs. Isolation (Self in relationships) 7. Middle Adulthood: Generativity vs. Stagnation (Self in terms of contribution to society) 8. Maturity / Old Age: Ego Integrity vs. Despair
